full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.—By this Rule Nisi the respondents were called upon to show cause as to why the order passed by the Member, Labour Appellate Tribunal on 21st December, 1972 in Appeal No.7 of 1972 reversing the decision of the First Labour Court of Bangladesh on 2nd May, 1972 in Industrial Dispute Case No. 3 of 1972 setting aside the order of dismissal of the petitioner, should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 5. On appeal of the judgment it appears that a preliminary objection was taken before the Appellate Tribunal that the appeal preferred by the employer was not competent in view of the fact that the dispute brought for adjudication under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 was not an "industrial dispute" and as such the decision of the Labour Court could not be termed as an "award". Against an award given by the Labour Court the statute provides an appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal and there is no provision of appeal against a decision of the Labour Court. This question has been dealt with by the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal at length. The sum and substance of the discussion of the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal is that—(i) The definition of the expression "industrial dispute" as defined in section 2(xiii) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, if properly construed with the aid of section 13 of the General Clauses Act, it will lead one to the conclusion that an individual dispute is covered by the expression "industrial dispute" ; (ii) in the Ordinance a clear line of demarcation has been maintained between industrial disputes which may be referred to, and which may be brought before a Labour Court ; but any dispute whether it is brought by an individual or brought by the workers collectively is an "industrial dispute''; and (iii) of the dispute of an individual works; man which has been brought to the Labour Court under section 34, is not an industrial dispute, the workman concerned will not get the protection of section 47, and consequently, the very purpose of section 34 will be defeated. On the basis of the above noted reasoning the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal arrived at the following conclusion :— 

 "In view of the discussion made above in the light of charges in law. I find that an individual dispute brought to a Labour Court by an application u/s. 34 is for the purpose of adjuration and determination, an industrial dispute ; consequently the order of the Labour Court disposing an application u/s. 34 is an award within the meaning of section 2(ii) of the Ordinance of 1969 and not a decision." 

 6. On the basis of the above conclusion the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal held that the application filed under section 34 by the dismissed worker, was an "industrial dispute" and as such the adjudication resulted in an "award". Therefore, the appeal before the Appellate Tribunal was competent. 

 The main basis of the decision of the Appellate Tribunal is the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(xiii) meaning.— 

 "Any dispute or difference between employers and employers or between employers and workmen or between workmen and workmen Which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employment or the conditions of work of any person." 

 7. According to the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal the definition includes an individual dispute as well, because, for the purpose of interpretation of the definition section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 will be applicable, which provides that words in the singular shall include the plural, and vice versa. And as such the word "workmen" includes "workman" and the work "employers" includes "employer". Practically this piece of reasoning has provided the main basis of the decision of the learned Member that an "individual dispute" comes within the definition of "industrial dispute", and as such the decision given by the Labour Court is as an award. In this context the learned Member has referred to the definition of "award" as contained in section 2(ii) of the Industrial Reliance Ordinance, 1969. According to this definition "award" means the determination by a Labour Court, Arbitrator or appellate Tribunal of any industrial dispute or any matter relating thereto and includes an interim award. Therefore, the learned Member concluded that since the dispute brought before the Labour Court was an industrial dispute, the decision given by the Labour Court thereon was an award and as such under section 37(3) it is appealable to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. 

 8. We have given our best consideration to the reasonings given by the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal and examined the different provisions of the Ordinance, and the decisions relied upon by him. In our opinion the learned Member is not correct in holding that the definition as contained section 2(xiii) support the contention that an "individual dispute" is included in the "industrial dispute" as contemplated in the Ordinance. In this context reference to section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 was not proper. It is correct that according to section 13 (2) of General Clauses Act 1897 "the words in the singular shall include the plural, and vice versa", but this process does not always help in giving the proper construction to the language of statute. Application of section 13 of the General Clauses Act is conditional. Sub-section (1) and (2) of section 13 of the General Clauses Act will be applicable "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context" of the Statute or Regulation. Section 13 does not provide that a word in singular is to be read as plural under all circumstances, but merely indicates the intention of the Legislature that the word may be read in plural whenever the circumstances require that it should be so construed. In order to get its true imp op it is necessary to view the enactment in retrospect, the reasons for enacting it, the evil it was to end and the objects it was to sub-serve. The Act has to be viewed as a whole and its intention determined by construing all constituent parts of the Act together and not by taking a detached section or to take on word here and another there. Section 13 begins with the words "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject, or context". Therefore the statute as a whole, is to be read to ascertain the scheme and object of the statute before applying this section. 

 9. In this context it will be convenient to refer to a decision of the High Bench Division in R.V. National Arbitration Tribunal and Another Exparte south Sheilds Corporation, (1951) 2 All. N.R.828. The learned Member of the appellate Tribunal also referred to this decision and quoted a paragraph from page 831 where Lord Goddard, C.J. discussed about interpretation of the definition of "trade dispute" with reference to an earlier decision of the Court in National Association of Local Government Officers Vs. Rolton Copn., (1942) 2 All. F.R. 435. The learned Member did not refer to the later portion of the report which contains the actual decision of the Court, in the case, which is more relevant for the purpose  of the present case. If may be mentioned that the definition of "industrial dispute" as quoted above is almost a copy of the definition of "trade dispute", occurring in the condition of Employment and National Arbitration Order, 1940 and Industrial disputes Order, 1951. The learned Chief Justice did not accept the interpretation sought to be given to the definition of "trade dispute" with the aid of Interpretation Act 1889 for the purpose of construing the statute itself which was under consideration. A page 833 the learned Chief Justice observed as follows :— 

 "When, therefore, we find in the definition of a dispute that it means a dispute between an "employer" in the singular and "workmen" in the plural it seems to us to be clear that the order is not contemplating he reference of a dispute which may arise between an employer and a single workman employed by him in connection with the terms of his employment, but is dealing with workmen as a class or body. The order of 1951 is, in our view intended to deal with disputes which affect either all the workmen in the service of an employer or a particular section of workmen in his employment. In our view, the whole tenor of the Order of 1951, and the fact that throughout the Order the word "employer" in the singular is used in conjunction with the word "workers" in the plural, indicates an intention that these words should be interpreted", literally and, in consequence, that s. 1(1) of the Interpretation Act, 1889, to which we have referred above, should not apply. Support for this construction is, we think to be found in the fact that a single workman cannot report a dispute, but the report must be by a trade union who normally act for workers as a body or for a class of workers". 

 10. Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 came into force on 13th November, 1969. The title of the Ordinance itself is significant. This indicates the purpose of the legislation. The preamble clarifies it further. It starts with these words— 

 “to amend and consolidate the law relating to the formation of trade unions, the regulation of relations between employers and workmen and the avoidance and settlement of any differences or disputes arising between them". 

 "whereas it is expedient to amend and consolidate the law relating to the formation of trade unions, the regulation of relations between employers and workmen and the avoidance and settlement of any difference or disputes arising between them or matters connected therewith and ancillary thereto and whereas the national interest of Pakistan in relation to the achievement of uniformity requires Central Legislation in the matter." 

 (2) The East Pakistan Labour Dispute Act, 1965. 

 (3) The West Pakistan Industrial Disputes Ordinance, 1965. 

 11. Section 35 contains the provision for constitution of Labour Courts and section 34 gives the jurisdiction to adjudicate industrial disputes, brought before it or referred to it by the Government. Some of the section of the Ordinance including sections 34 and 35 were amended on 17th October, 1970. If the original statute as passed on 13th November, 1969 is compared with the amended one, it appears that the scope of adjudication by the Labour Court has been enlarged, but in spite of the amendment the object and purpose of the legislation, namely, regulation of relations between employers and workmen has not been changed, Therefore it is difficult to accept the contention that in view of the amendment of section 34 of the Ordinance, individual dispute has been brought within the category of disputes termed as "industrial dispute". Section 34 before amendment was like this— 

 "Any party to an industrial dispute relating to matter arising out of any right guaranteed or secured to an employer or work an by or under any law for the time being in force or an award or settlement may apply to the Labour Court for adjudication of the dispute". 

 It appears from the amended section 34 that an individual employer or workman may apply to the Labour Court for enforcement of any right, etc. which may be "an individual dispute" or in a particular case when other requirements are fulfilled may be an “industrial dispute”. According to the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal any dispute brought before the Labour Court is an industrial dispute, and there is no distinction in the adjudication of such a dispute. This view of the learned Member is based on his interpretation of the definition of 'Industrial disputes" with the aid of section 13 of the General Clauses Act. Now let us see what is the principle of interpretation of definition clause and how far it intrinsically aids interpretation of the statute. 

 14. Following the principles of interpretation discussed above let us examine as to whether the learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal has followed correct principle in interpreting the provisions of section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 with the aid of the definition of "industrial dispute" by putting an extended meaning to the definition clause. The language of the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(xiii) is similar as contained in the definition of the expression "industrial dispute" as defined in section 2 (k) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 and section 2 (h) of the Industrial Disputes Ordinance, 1959. The following was the definition of "industrial dispute" contained in section 2(k) of Industrial Dispute Act, 1947. 

 "Any dispute or difference between employers and employers or between employers and workmen or between, workmen and workmen which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employment of the conditions of work of any person." 

 The definition as contained in the previous labour statutes have already received interpretation from different Superior Courts and the preponderance of the decision is not in favour of putting any extended meaning to the definition. The legislature while framing the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 did not consider it necessary to change the language of the definitions. It should be presumed that the legislature was fully aware of the chain of decisions based on the interpretation of the expression "industrial dispute" occurring in the previous labour law. The legislature did not consider it necessary to amend the definition even when amending several including sections 34 and 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 and thereby enlarging the scope of section 34. 

 15. Now let us see how the definition of the expression "industrial dispute" as contained in the previous statutes, namely, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Industrial Disputes Ordinance, 1959 and the East Pakistan Labour Dispute Act, 1965 has been interpreted by the different Superior Courts of the Sub continent. We have already noted above that the definition of "industrial dispute" contained in section 2(xiii) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 is similar in language as contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Industrial Disputes Ordinance, 1959 and East Pakistan Labour Disputes Act, 1965. Let us examine as to how this definition has been interpreted by the different superior Courts in the Sub-continent. Let us start with a decision of a Division Bench of the Madras High Court which has been followed by the different High Courts and got the approval of the Supreme Court of India. In the case of Kandan Textile Ltd. Vs. The Industrial Tribunal and others reported in AIR 1951 (Madras) 616, where in the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2 (k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 came up for consideration, it has been held by the Division Bench consisting of Rajamanner C.J. and Mack, J, that a dismissed worker cannot, by making a demand for rein-statement create an industrial dispute. The learned Chief Justice, however, remarked— 

 "I must confess that the language of the definition of "industrial dispute" is so wide that, giving the words their ordinary meaning, even a dispute between an employer and one of the workmen or between one workman and another workman which is connected with one or other of the matters mentioned therein would fall within the definition". 

 16. It appears from a decision of the Patna High Court in the case of K.H. Gandhi Vs. R N P. Singha and another, AIR, 1958 Patna 320 that the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2 (k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was considered in connection with a controversy as to whether the definition of "industrial dispute" includes an "individual dispute". The learned Judges of the Division Bench consisting of Rai and Singha. J. held that "Industrial dispute" as defined in section 2(k) must be construed to mean not a dispute between an individual workman and the management but a dispute which though it may originate in an action with regard to an individual workman has developed into a dispute in which the majority of the workmen in the establishment are interested. This view was taken by the learned Judges on the basis of an earlier decision of that Court in the case of New India Assurance Co. Vs. Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, Dhanbad reported in AIR 1953 Patna 321. In these decisions the decision of the Madras High Court mentioned above was followed. This view has been reaffirmed in subsequent decisions of that court, namely, South Bihar Sugar Mill Ltd. Bista Vs. State of Bihar. AIR 1956 Patna 274 and in Ahmad All Vs Sia Saran, AIR 1961 Patna, 342. 

 17. The definition of "Industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(k) in Industrial Dispute Act. 1947 came up for consideration before a. Single Judge Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case of News Papers Ltd, Allahahad Vs. Industrial Tribunal U P. Allahabad and others, AIR 1954 Allahabad 516. Bhargava, J. interpreted the definition clause with the aid of section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and held that an industrial dispute covers an industrial dispute and as such an individual dispute can be brought before the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The learned Judge did not follow the decision of the Madras High Court referred to above but with reference to the remark of C.J., Rajamannar, quoted above, held as follows :— 

 "I consequently held that an industrial dispute can come into existence even if the parties to the dispute be a single employer and a single workman provided, of course, other conditions are satisfied. In this case, there was no argument that the dispute was of such a nature that it could not be held to be an industrial dispute. Clearly it was not a private dispute between two individuals but was a dispute relating to the employment or non-employment of the workman in an industry run by the petitioner". 

 Mitter J. of the Calcutta High Court followed the Madras decision in the case J. Chowdhury Vs. M.C. Banarjee, 55 Cal. Weekly Notes 256. In this case a reference made by the Government in a case of a dismissed employee was held incompetent, because the dispute in question could not and was not an industrial dispute. 

 18. The difference of opinion in the different High Courts in India, about the interpretation of the definition clause as contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act 1947 has since been settled by the Supreme Court of India in the case Central Provinces Transport Services Ltd. Vs. Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, 1958 Supreme Court Reports 956. In this decision the different views on the question whether a dispute of an individual workman is covered by the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947, have been discussed. The decisions have been classified in three group of cases has taken the view that a dispute which concerns only the rights of individual workers, can not be held to be an industrial dispute. This is the opinion first expressed in Kandan Textiles Vs. Industrial Tribunal AIR 1951 Madras 611. This decision has been approved in Manager, United Commercial Bank Ltd Vs. Commissioner of Labour. AIR 1951 Madras 141. This decision has been followed by the Calcutta High Court in J. Chowdhury Vs, M. C. Banerjee 55 C.W.N.256. Second Group of cases has taken the view that a dispute between an employer and a single employee can be an industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k). This view was taken by the Allahabad High Court in News papers Ltd. Allahabad Vs. State Industrial Tribunal, U.P. AIR 1954 Allahabad 516. The third group of cases which is larger in number, has taken the view that a dispute between an employer and a single employee can not peruse be an industrial dispute but it may become one, if it is taken up by the Union or a considerable number of workmen. This opinion has been expressed by Bose, J. in Bilash Chanda Mitra Vs. Blamer Tawries & Co., AIR 1958 Cal. 613 ; by Ramaswami and Sarjoo Prasad, JJ. in New India Assurance Co. Vs. Central Government Industrial Tribunal, AIR 1953 Patna 321 This Supreme Court summed up the discussion as follows : 

 "The preponderance of judicial opinion is clearly in favour of the last of the three views stated above, and there is considerable reason behind it. Notwithstanding that the language of S. 2(k) is wide enough to cover a dispute between an employeer and a single employee, the scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion, to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workman as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of an adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen". 

 The Supreme Court, however, refrained from expressing final opinion on the question whether a dispute simpliciter between employer and a workman would be an industrial dispute within section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 

 19. The question, namely, a dispute between an employer and a single workman in an industry again came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of India in the News Papers Ltd. Vs. The State Industrial Tribunal, U.P.957 Supreme Court Reports 754. It may be noted that the appeal before the Supreme Court was against the judgment and decree of the Allahabad High Court in Special Appeal No.8 of 1959 arising out of the judgment and decree passed by Bharjana J. reported in AIR 1954 Allahabad 516, already discussed earlier. The decision of Bharjana, J. upheld in appeal by the Division Bench, has been set aside. 

 20. In this case the dispute was brought before the Industrial Tribunal in the following circumstances —Tojammel Hussain, respondent No. 3 was employed as a steno-typist by the appellant company. He was dismissed on allegations of incompetence under the standing orders of the Company. The appellant company alleged that the dismissal was welcomed by his co-workers and other workmen in the employ of the company, and they made no grievance of it, nor did they espouse his cause. The case of the worker was not taken up by any union of workers of the appellants company nor by any of the unions of workmen employed in similar or allied trades but the U.P. working journalists union. Lucknow, with which respondent No. 3 had no connection whatsoever, took the matter to the Conciliation Board, Allahabad., Ultimately the U.P. Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal by a notification; the preparatory works of which are: Whereas an Industrial dispute in respect of the matters hereinafter specified exists between the concern known as News Paper Ltd. Allahabad and its workmen ; and whereas in the opinion of the Governor it is necessary so to do for the maintenance of public order and for maintaining employment ..." 

 "whether the services of Sri Tojammel Hussain, Lino operator was wrongly terminated by the Management..." In this decision the Supreme Court of India reviewed practically all the relevant cases on the relevant English Labour Laws, Australian Labour Laws and Indian Labour Laws wherein the scope of "industrial dispute" has been considered. After considering the cases of different Superior Courts of different countries viz vis Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Supreme Court disapproved the decisions where in It was held that a dispute raised by an individual workman is within an industrial dispute. The Supreme Court approved the view taken in the decisions that a dispute between an employer and a single workman does not fall within the definition of "industrial dispute, But if in a dispute concerning an individual. workman the workmen as a body or a considerable section of them make common cause with the individual workman, then such a dispute would be an industrial dispute. 

 21. The Supreme Court of India in the above noted decision discussed about the scope and object of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947. In this context it followed the opinion expressed by the same court earlier in D.N. Banerjee Vs. P R. Mukharjee and others, 1953 Supreme Court Reports, 310 wherein the expression "industrial dispute' as defined in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 was discussed and the Court expressed the opinion that it conveys the meaning to the ordinary mind that the dispute must be such as would affect large groups of workmen and employees ranged on opposite sides... But at the same time having regard to the modern conditions of society where capital and labour have organised themselves into grousp for the purpose of .fighting their dispute and settling them on the basis of the theory that union is strength and collective bargaining has come to stay, a single employee's case might develop into an industrial dispute when as often happens it is taken up by the trade union of which he is a member and there is a concerted demand by the employees for redress". 

 "This view which has been re-affirmed by the Court in several later decisions recognises the great importance in modern industrial life of collective bargaining between the workman and the employers. It is well known how before the days of collective bargaining labour was at a great disadvantage in obtaining reasonable terms for contracts of service from his employer. As trade unions developed in the country and collective bargaining became a rule the employers found it necessary and convenient to deal with the representation of workman  instead of individual workman not only for making of modification of contracts but in the matter of taking disciplinary action against one or more workmen and as regards all other disputes. The necessary corollary to this is that the individual workman is at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the union. The union or those workmen who have by their sponsoring turned the individual dispute into an industrial dispute, can therefore claim to have a say in the conduct of the proceedings before the tribunal. 

 The definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 came up for consideration in the case of Pakistan Tobacco Company. Ltd. Vs. Pakistan Tobacco Company Employers Union Dacca; reported in 13 DLR (SC) 280. The question for consideration was as to whether in view of the expression "any person" occurring in section 2(k) "salesman" could be treated as "workman" and consequently the dispute between the workers and the employer over that matter could be treated as an "industrial dispute". 

 It has been held in the said decision that the definition clause should be strictly construed for the purpose of interpreting the different provisions of the statute, and there is no scope for giving a wide meaning of the definition to include "any person" of the establishment coming within the scope of definition of workman. In this, context Cornelius, C.J. while dealing with the purpose and the scope of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 observed as follows :— 

 "It is undeniable that the main principle of the Industrial Dispute Act is to supply means by which overall harmonious relation may be maintained in the field of industry, not only between employers and their workmen, but between workmen and workmen in the same establishment, and even between employers and employers in the same industry, or perhaps even in other industries. These categories relate to differences at three different levels, but all of three are addressed to the same overriding necessity, that disputes which had arisen among these two categories, viz, of employers on one side and workman on the other, should be harmoniously composed through the intervention of an independent Board or Tribunal and sometimes by reference to a Court." 

 24. A Division Bench of the Dacca High Court consisting of Sattar and Sekander Ali, JJ. Md. Ataullah Vs. P.I.D.C. and an other, 14 DLR (Dacca) 654, where the definition of "industrial dispute" as contained in section 2(h) of the Industrial Dispute Ordinance which is similar in language as section 2 k) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 came up for consideration in connection with a case where a worker while employed as a permanent Mechanic in the Sugar Mills of the P.I.D.C. (Respondent) governed as per terms and conditions of appointment, the respondents No. 2 (the Manager of the Mills) illegally terminated his service, expressed a clear opinion that a dispute of an individual workman in this case a dismissed workman cannot be said to amount to an "industrial dispute". The relevant portion of the decision is quoted below :— 

 "Having examined the relevant provisions of the Ordinance we fail to see how an individual worker can initiate a proceeding thereunder or how the cause of an individual worker can be said to amount to an "industrial dispute" unless that is made an issue, i.e. a common cause, by the entire body of workers or group of them and thus threatens to affect the working of the establishment concern". 

 25. The definition of "industrial dispute" contained in section 2(h) of the Industrial Disputes Ordinance, 1959 came up for consideration before a Division Bench of Lahore High Court in the case of Jalal Din Vs. Orient Match Company Ltd. and others, reported in PLD 1968 Lah. 269. The Bench consisting of Sardar Muhammad Iqbal and Muhammad Akram, JJ. discussed at length the principle of interpretation of a definition clause for the purpose of finding out the object of a statute with reference to the different provisions of the labour law under consideration, and a number of decisions relevant for the case. The learned Judges did not accept the interpretation of the definition clause sought to be given by applying section 13 of the General Clauses Act that the definition clause should be construed so as to hold that "industrial dispute" includes "individual dispute". 

 "A labour Court shall –(a) adjudicate and determine an industrial dispute which has been referred to or brought before under this Ordinance : "when an individual dispute is brought by a workman before a Labour Court, for instance by a dismissed workman, the decision given by the Labour Court can not be termed as "aware'. The learned Member of the Appellate Tribunal has taken the view that both the provisions, viz., under section 23 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and in section 34 of the Industrial Relations, Ordinance, 1969 are available to an aggrieved workman and it is for him to choose which of the two courses he wants to adopt. Apparently this view does not appear to be arroneous. It has also not been contended in the other way from the bar. However, we are not repressing our final opinion on this question. In any view of the matter, when an application is filed by a workman for relief in his "individual dispute", the dispute cannot be entertained by the Labour Court as an "industrial dispute", and the decision of the labour Court does not become an "award." This view gets full support from section 43 of the Ordinance. An individual dispute brought by a workman is adjudicated as an individual dispute, and it terminates in a decision. Section 35 the scope of adjudication of the Labour Court has been widened without making any distinction about the scope of adjudication in respect of an "industrial dispute" brought before it by the collective Bargaining Agent or an employer or workman or referred by the Government under section 32(3) or section 33(2) of the Ordinance. Section 43 of the Ordinance has been slightly amended but without changing its character. The amended section 43 clearly indicates the intention of the Legislature. It provides in a very clear language that no industrial dispute shall be deemed to exist unless it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or an employer. This section is a material factor in determining whether it is an individual dispute or industrial dispute. 

 27. This question may be tested from another aspect. The Labour Court constituted under section 35 of the Ordinance, is also the forum for filing a complaint under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. When an application is filed under section 34 a workman against his dismissal by his employer the matter is to be adjudicated according to the provisions of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965, because. there is no appropriate provisions in the Ordinance for giving the necessary reliefs. Therefore a dismissed workman, in view of the amendment of section 34 of the Ordinance, may file an application under section 34, but the matter, for all practical purposes, is to be treated as a matter as provided in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders Act, 1965. And the adjudication of the matter terminates in a decision and not in an "award" Considering the various aspect of the case, we are of opinion that the view taken by the learned Member, of the Appellate Tribunal is not correct. If the interpretation given by the learned Member is accepted as correct, then the whole purpose and object of the Ordinance will be defeated. In our opinion the dispute brought by the petitioner before the Labour Court was an individual dispute and the adjudication terminated in a "decision" and consequently the appeal before the Appellate Tribunal was incompetent. 

 29. With reference to this order of the Labour Court the learned Advocates of the petitioner submits that the petitioner was allowed to withdraw the application with the liberty to file a new application under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1968. Therefore, the cause of action of the petitioner contained when section 34 was amended on 17th October, 1970, and as such the petitioner was entitled to file an application under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, and there is no scope for contending that the same was barred by resjudicata. We accept the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, and we hold that the application filed by the petitioner under section 34 of Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 was not barred by resjudicata.
